question.text: Does pediatric housestaff experience influence tests ordered for infants in the neonatal intensive care unit?
question.context: To assess the relationship between the experience of pediatric housestaff and tests ordered on infants in the neonatal intensive care unit (ICU). Prospective, cohort study over one full academic year. One academic Level III neonatal intensive care nursery. Data were collected prospectively on all 785 infants admitted to the neonatal ICU from July 1993 to June 1994. These infants were cared for by 14 different categorical pediatric housestaff. Our neonatal ICU has either a resident or an intern on-call by himself/herself at night, affording us a natural setting to compare intern vs. resident test ordering. The outcomes of interest were number of arterial blood gases, radiographs, and electrolytes ordered per infant by the on-call pediatric houseofficer, as tabulated the morning after the call night. Control variables included the severity-of-illness of the individual infant (using the Neonatal Therapeutic Intervention Scoring System), the workload of the houseofficer (number of patients, number of admissions), and supervision (rounding frequency and on-call attending). Controlling for the severity-of-illness of the infant, the workload on the call night, and supervision with multiple linear regression, we found that interns ordered significantly (p = .02) greater numbers of arterial blood gases per infant than residents, amounting to some 0.33 blood gases per infant per call night (3.22 vs. 2.89 arterial blood gases per infant per night). This increase of 0.33 blood gases per infant amounts to interns ordering $169 more arterial blood gases per call night at our institution. There was no difference between interns and residents in ordering radiographs or electrolytes.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that interns ordered significantly more arterial blood gases per infant than residents, even after controlling for infant severity, workload, and supervision. This suggests that the experience level of the house officer influences test ordering practices.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Interns ordered significantly (p = .02) greater numbers of arterial blood gases per infant than residents.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors might influence test ordering, the statistically significant difference in arterial blood gas orders between interns and residents, even after controlling for other variables, strongly suggests that experience plays a role. Other factors like patient severity or workload could potentially influence test ordering, but the difference in arterial blood gas orders is the most direct and significant finding.

This statistically significant difference, after controlling for infant severity, workload, and supervision, indicates that pediatric housestaff experience does influence test ordering in the neonatal ICU.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The p-value of.02 for the difference in arterial blood gas orders between interns and residents, after controlling for confounding variables, provides strong evidence that experience level affects test ordering.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses needed - this is a straightforward statistical analysis question. The key consideration was whether the observed difference was statistically significant after controlling for relevant variables, which it was.

This demonstrates a measurable influence of housestaff experience on test ordering. qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Interns ordered 0.33 more arterial blood gases per infant per call night (p = .02), amounting to $169 more per night, after controlling for confounders.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Radiographs and electrolytes were not different between interns and residents, so they were not a confounding factor; the effect was specific to arterial blood gases, not general test ordering.
